key_bets: Energy confinement time scales as τₑ ~ R² in a D-He3 dipole at meter-scale radius, enabling Q > 1 at orbital device scale
D-D side reactions self-breed He3 via tritium decay at rates sufficient to sustain continuous commercial fuel supply without external procurement
End-to-end power beaming efficiency (fusion → proton deceleration → DC → microwave transmitter → atmosphere → rectenna → grid) exceeds ~30% at multi-MW scale
D-He3 ion temperatures of 50–100 keV are achievable in a levitated dipole geometry despite being 5–10× higher than D-T requirements
A complete fusion reactor spacecraft (HTS coil, heating, power conversion, thermal management) can be packaged within 5,000–15,000 kg for Falcon 9 launch
Space-qualified HTS coil with on-board cryocooler can maintain ~20–30 K operation in LEO radiation environment for multi-year orbital lifetime
Direct conversion of 14.7 MeV protons at the dipole separatrix is achievable at commercially viable efficiency
eliminated_costs: CAS 21–23 first wall, blanket, shield, and vacuum vessel — eliminated by orbital deployment with no structural containment
CAS 24–26 turbine plant, electrical plant, and heat rejection — replaced by direct conversion and power beaming (no thermal cycle)
Tritium breeding infrastructure — Li-6 enrichment, FLiBe/Li-metal handling, and tritium processing eliminated by aneutronic D-He3 fuel
14 MeV neutron shielding materials (tungsten, WC cermet, B₄C) — eliminated; D-D side-reaction neutrons radiate into space
Conventional site and building costs — no terrestrial reactor building, foundation, or containment structure
novel_costs: Launch cost to LEO as primary CAPEX driver (~$2,700/kg Falcon 9, ~$13–40M/unit at 5,000–15,000 kg spacecraft mass)
Power beaming ground infrastructure — rectenna fields at ~$2M/MW (GW-class GEO SPS analogue), 10×13 km receiving area per GW
Helium-3 fuel procurement at ~$28–34M/kg market price, or self-breeding infrastructure with 12.3-year tritium decay cycle
Direct conversion hardware for 14.7 MeV protons — no commercial supply chain, first-of-kind space-qualified manufacturing
Orbital O&M: debris mitigation, radiation hardening, cryocooler/radiator thermal management, replacement logistics with no EVA analogue

risks.description: No energy conversion pathway specified — direct conversion and power beaming efficiency chain entirely undefined; delivered power formally undefined making LCOE uncalculable

He3 supply fundamentally constrained — global production ~1.8–2.7 kg/year, market price ~$30M/kg, subject to DOE/DHS/DOD export controls and government rationing; self-breeding pathway undemonstrated in dipole geometry
Energy confinement scaling law unknown for dipole geometry — OpenStar explicitly states 'no such model exists'; D-He3 requires ~10× higher triple product than D-T
D-He3 confinement physics requires 50–100 keV ion temperatures — 2–3 orders of magnitude above LDX/RT-1 experimental heritage of a few hundred eV
Power beaming end-to-end efficiency realistically ~14% with phased-array steering (<20% TX × 89% beam × 80% rectenna); below ~20% threshold makes terrestrial competition impossible regardless of Q
No heating method disclosed — recirculating power fraction unanchored; high fraction could render concept non-viable independent of other parameters
Zephyr is pre-prototype (~2 employees, YC F25 2025) with no technical papers, patents, grants, or plasma parameter disclosures — entire public technical content fits one launch page
Orbital HTS coil lifetime under Van Allen belt proton/electron bombardment, thermal cycling, and magnetic stress is unvalidated at fusion-relevant field strengths
Space-qualified cryocooler and radiator sizing for ~20–30 K coil temperature in LEO thermal environment has no precedent at fusion coil scale
Regulatory dual-track risk — IAEA/UN COPUOS oversight for nuclear material in orbit plus DOE/DHS/DOD export controls on He3/tritium procurement; policy barrier unresolvable by technology alone
Capital cost structure has no published analogue — CAS 10-LCOE framework does not apply; free-form orbital spacecraft cost model required
Plant capacity factor undefined — no orbital fusion O&M precedent; debris/radiation events could drive significant unplanned downtime offsetting steady-state advantage
Direct conversion hardware has no commercial supply chain — only reference is 1970s Venetian blind DEC (never manufactured at scale, never space-qualified)

Competitive benchmark uncertainty — Zephyr cites ITER ($650M/MW) but relevant benchmarks are SPS parity ($200–500/MWh) and terrestrial fusion parity ($50–150/MWh), requiring different development paths
